notes.title: 받침
notes.text: A 받침 is the consonant at the bottom of a syllable block (the ㄱ in 각, the ㄹ in 말). Many 받침 sound alike at the end of a word: ㄷ ㅅ ㅈ ㅊ ㅌ ㅎ all end in a stopped "t" (옷, 낮, 꽃). When the next syllable starts with a vowel, the 받침 slides over: 옷이 sounds like [오시].

notes.title: 해석 vs 번역
notes.text: 번역 is translating a text into another language. 해석 is interpreting — making sense of something. Learners often say 해석해 주세요 to ask "what does this mean?" Interpreting speech out loud is 통역.

notes.title: 학원
notes.text: Many Korean kids go to private after-school academies (학원) for English, math, piano, taekwondo and more — sometimes until late at night. The homeroom teacher is 담임 선생님, and report cards (성적표) come out every semester (학기).

notes.title: University life
notes.text: 입학 (starting school) and 졸업 (graduating) are big family events in Korea, celebrated with flowers and photos. 신입생 = freshman, 졸업생 = graduate, 대학원 = graduate school, 등록금 = tuition, 장학금 = scholarship. Students from abroad are 유학생.

notes.title: 기억하다 vs 기억나다
notes.text: 기억하다 = to remember (keep in mind): 제 이름 기억하세요? 기억나다 = something comes back to you: 아, 이제 기억났어요! To say you can't recall: 기억이 안 나요. Korean high-school trips (수학여행) often go to Gyeongju, the old Silla capital.

notes.title: How sure are you?
notes.text: From most to least sure: 틀림없어요 (no doubt) → 확실해요 (certain) → 분명히 (clearly) → 아마 (probably) → 글쎄요 (well… I'm not sure). Fried chicken and beer (치맥) is Korea's classic way to celebrate.
